newsitem.title: UK: Buying emerging markets? Use the sneaker indicator.
newsitem.headline: Buying emerging markets? Use the sneaker indicator.

text.p: Investors seeking a sure bet in the uncertain world of emerging market investment should use their feet -- and follow the Nike Indicator.

Analysis of Nike's production pattern found that every country in which the company had produced sneakers had seen high, long-term economic growth, emerging markets house Robert Fleming's global emerging markets research team said in a report released on Monday.
"It is widely said that using economists to figure out where an economy is headed is like driving a car by looking in the rear-view mirror," the report by analyst Li Tong said.
Nike is one of the most successful manufacturing companies in the United States, but outsources most of its products to contractors in Asia, and not just because of low labour costs.
Management at Nike said criteria used in selecting a country included political stability, quality of labour, infrastructure, government policy, customs duties and quotas.
Nike first produced in Japan in 1972, then moved to Korea and Taiwan in 1975, and from 1987 began to rapidly expand its production in Thailand, China and Indonesia.
About 70 percent of its sneakers are now produced in China and Indonesia after departing from Thailand.

Tong said Thailand should welcome Nike's departure, as it indicated that the economy was successful. "Wage rates go up because workers have learned skills (like going on strike). Nike's departure indicates that the country is at a new stage of development."
Tong said it showed Thailand was ready to move from manufacturing sneakers to semi-conductors.
"Investors should note that Japan and Korea both saw tremendous growth in their automobile industries after Nike left."

While China and Indonesia are Nike's current stars, Vietnam's economic future looks bright, at least according to the Nike Indicator. The country will account for 10 percent of sneaker production in 1997 from two percent in 1996.
But India, despite cheap labour, is not yet on Nike's list for large-scale production.

Tong also noticed a correlation between Nike's production value and stock market indices, at least in Thailand, "pushing the analysis to the limits of applicability for investors". A similar relationship appeared in Korea, where a market lull coincided with Nike pulling out of the country.
